```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
install.packages("factoextra")

#for PCAs
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)
library(corrplot) # For correlation plots
library(FactoMineR) # For PCA
library(factoextra) # For PCA plots
library(GGally) # For multiple plots

#for random forest
library(rsample)
library(rpart)
library(rpart.plot)
library(randomForest)
library(caret)
library(class) 
```

## Exploratory data analysis

Data are from: Mesquita, Daniel O., et al. “Life history data of lizards of the world (Ecological Archives E096-058).” Ecology 96.2 (2015): 594-594.

Looks like there are lots of NAs in our data, particularly in the measured observation. Reproduction, foraging, distribution, and habitat all have lots of data. Of measured data, also mean clutch size, clutch frequency, and mean.f.svl

```{r looking at trends}
#read in dataset
lizard <- read.csv("data/raw/lizard.csv")

head(lizard)
tail(lizard) #oooh empty rows at the end to delete!
dim(lizard) #740 -> 737 obs
names(lizard) #column names
str(lizard) #variable type. some issues here. chr that should be num

#then let's look at NAs - lots!
#best ones look like family (etc), repro, foraging, distribution, habitat, mean.clutch size, clutch frequency, mean.f.svl.adults
colSums(is.na(lizard))

#let's look at what we do know, to try to choose a balanced design
table(lizard$Family) #uneven distribution for sure. 
table(lizard$Mode.of.reproduction) #lots, but not balanced
table(lizard$Foraging.Mode) #well balanced!
table(lizard$Distribution) #also well balanced!
table(lizard$Prefered.Habitat.Type) #not well balanced at all, beware. could maybe clump?
summary(lizard$Mean.Clutch.Size) #huh. probably a few high outliers. only 4 NAs
table(lizard$Clutch.Frequency) #weird low outliers, should this not be number of clutches per year? weird if so. maybe needs to be changed to categorical?
```

```{r cleaning data}
#ok first let's remove the empty rows at the end
lizard <- lizard[1:(nrow(lizard)-3), ]

#now let's change SD Female adult weight to numeric.
#hmm, .upon looking at the data, it seems that the issue is that one of the obs has a comma where it should have a decimal. let's fix that!
 lizard %>%
   mutate(SD.Female.adult.weight..g. = as.numeric(
     str_replace(SD.Female.adult.weight..g., ",", "."))) -> lizard

#let's save these data in a clean lizard file
write.csv(lizard, "data/working/lizard-clean.csv", row.names = FALSE)

```


Let's add climate data from CHELSA, particularly annual precip, precip seasonality, temp seasonality, mean annual temp, and bioregions
```{r adding climate data}
#these data are downloaded from CHELSA, applied in QGIS, joined with original lizard, and then exported to csv
#lizard <- read.csv("data/working/lizard-climate.csv")

#can read in new lizard-working from curro, that includes lizard-climate and things he's added
lizard <- read.csv("data/working/lizard-climate.csv")

#check new variable
str(lizard)

#quick clean of variable type!
#let's change clutch frequency to be a categorical variable 
lizard %>%
  mutate(Clutch.Frequency = case_when(
    Clutch.Frequency <= 1 ~ "<= 1", #here we're including those that are less than one. can we do that?
    Clutch.Frequency == 2 ~ "2")) %>%
  mutate(Clutch.Frequency = factor(Clutch.Frequency)) -> lizard

```

## Visualizing

```{r intro visualizing}
hist(lizard$Mean.Clutch.Size)
hist(lizard$Mean.F.SVL.adults..mm.)
#ggplot(lizard, aes(x = Clutch.Frequency)) + geom_bar()

#to see relationship of repro mode and clutch size. not as obvious as i thought
ggplot(lizard, aes(x = Mode.of.reproduction,
                   y = Mean.Clutch.Size,
                   fill = Mode.of.reproduction)) + geom_boxplot()

ggplot(lizard, aes(x = Distribution,
                   y = Clutch.Frequency,
                   fill = Distribution)) + geom_plot()

ggplot(lizard, aes(x = Family,
                   fill = Mode.of.reproduction)) + geom_bar()

ggplot(lizard, aes(x = Distribution,
                   fill = Clutch.Frequency)) + geom_bar()

```

```{r removing unecessary columns}
##let's look at how the variables correlate to see if we can cut some.

lizard %>% 
  select_if(is.numeric) %>% #select just the quantitative variables
  cor(use = "complete.obs") %>% #this let's us get around NAs
  corrplot() #and plot

#if we focus on variables that are >=0.8, we can decide if some of them are related and could be removed
#even though lat and long are highly correlated, we'll keep both. I think we can get rid of all SDs, since we're limited by sample size. The sample sizes are also all similar, and since I'm guessing they're just used to calculate the averages, we can remove those. F.SVL at maturity and Mean.F.SVL. adults have a super high correlation - let's remove the at maturity one, since it's just the smallest reproductive female. clutches per year and clutch frequency are essentially the same thing, so let's cut clutches per year since we have fewer observations for it. phew!

#let's cut the columns we tagged
lizard %>% 
  select(-fid, -SD.Female.adult.weight..g., -Sample.Size.Female.adult.weight, -SD.F.SVL.adults..mm., -Sample.size.Mean.F.SVL.adults, -Sample.size.Clutch.Size., -Clutches.per.year, -F.SVL.at.maturity..mm., -RCM) -> lizard
```

##Exploratory statistics

Ok, first let's look at some real simple things
```{r simple stats}
#relationship between Distribution and Foraging mode
table(lizard$Distribution, lizard$Foraging.Mode) -> tab_forage

chisq.test(tab_forage)
#looking very significant!

#what about Distribution and Habitat?
table(lizard$Distribution, lizard$Prefered.Habitat.Type) -> tab_habitat

chisq.test(tab_habitat)
#also extremely significant

#what if we tried a glm?
lizard$Mode.of.reproduction <- factor(
  lizard$Mode.of.reproduction,
  levels = c("Oviparous", "Viviparous"))

lizard$Distribution <- factor(
  lizard$Distribution,
  levels = c("Tropical", "Temperate"))

glm(Mode.of.reproduction ~ Distribution, data = lizard, family = binomial(link = "logit")) -> model_q1

summary(model_q1)

#with species as random effect
library(lme4)

model_q1_mixed <- glmer(
  Mode.of.reproduction ~ Distribution + (1 | Species),
  data = lizard,
  family = binomial)

summary(model_q1_mixed)

```


Let's look at a pca to see if we can get at explaining family from some of these numerical stats
```{r exploratory PCAs}
#first, looking again at families
sort(table(lizard$Family), decreasing = TRUE) -> family_counts #plenty here with very few individuals, so let's cut our dataset down to....the top 13

top13_families <- names(family_counts)[1:13]

lizard %>%
  filter(Family %in% top13_families) -> lizard_top13

sort(table(lizard_top13$Family), decreasing = TRUE)

#ok, then, looking at which numerical variables we have...
str(lizard_top13)
colSums(is.na(lizard_top13))

#we should choose those we're interested in, that have the fewest NAs
lizard_top13 %>%
  select(
    Mean.F.SVL.adults..mm.,
    Clutch.Frequency,
    Mean.Clutch.Size) %>%
  na.omit() -> lizard_clean

PCA(lizard_clean, 
    scale.unit = TRUE, # Option to center and scale data (useless here)
    ncp = 3, # number of variables
    graph = FALSE) -> pca_lizard

summary(pca_lizard)

fviz_eig(pca_lizard, choice = "variance")

fviz_pca_var(pca_lizard,
             axes = c(1, 2), col.var="cos2")

```

Ok, let's try running a random forest to predict family. Whelp, barring some trouble with dividing the families into proportional splits, the random forest was decent at predicting - 82%. but some of the families with fewer individuals are just much worse at predicting. So in the end, you probably could use a whole bunch of characteristics to guess family. but would that be useful? It seems more likely that you would be able to tell family visually, and you might want to predict other characteristics instead. 
```{r random forest Family}
#let's keep the variables that have the fewest NAs
colSums(is.na(lizard_top13))

lizard_top13 %>%
  select(
    Family,
    Mean.F.SVL.adults..mm.,
    Mean.Clutch.Size,
    Clutch.Frequency,
    Mode.of.reproduction,
    Distribution,
    Foraging.Mode,
    Prefered.Habitat.Type) %>%
  na.omit() %>% 
  as.data.frame()-> rf_lizard

# Check how many observations remain after removing NAs
nrow(rf_lizard)

#change Family to categorical
rf_lizard %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.character), as.factor),
         Family = as.factor(Family)) -> rf_lizard

#here we go!
set.seed(123)

split_lizard <- initial_split(rf_lizard, prop = 0.75, strata = "Family") #this allows us to split our dataset into training and testing datasets
train_lizard <- analysis(split_lizard)
test_lizard  <- assessment(split_lizard)

# Check the sizes
dim(train_lizard)
nrow(test_lizard)

# Check family representation in each set. hmmm, something is not right for sphaerodactylidae and xenosauridae. what to do?
table(train_lizard$Family)
table(test_lizard$Family)

##tune the forest
params_CV <- trainControl(method = "cv", verboseIter = FALSE, number = 10)

caret::train(
  Family ~ ., #all variables
  data = train_lizard,
  method = "rf", #using random forest
  metric = "Accuracy",
  trControl = params_CV,
  tuneGrid = expand.grid(mtry = 1:7), #mtry here
  ntree = 500) -> predictor_forest

predictor_forest #final model! most optimized! mtry = 4

plot(predictor_forest)

rf_cv_predictions <- predict(predictor_forest, newdata = select(test_lizard, -Family))
rf_cv_confusion <- confusionMatrix(rf_cv_predictions, test_lizard$Family) 
rf_cv_confusion

```

On second thought, random forest to predict family is maybe not as useful, since we usually have family but don't often have the other measurements. so what if we do a random forest to predict a different variable, say mean clutch size, based on family. 
```{r random forest Mean.Clutch.Size}
#random forest can't deal with NAs. so I really think we should run two version of this code, one with all the variables of interest, and one without the ones with a bunch of NAs

#let's divide our df into env and ecological variables
#environmental
environmental_vars <- c("mean_annual_temperature", "annual_precip", "precip_seasonality", "temp_seasonality","Latitude", "bioregion")

#ecological_all
ecological_all_vars <- c("Average.Female.adult.weight..g.","Mean.F.SVL.adults..mm.","Offspring.SVL..mm.", "Mode.of.reproduction", "Clutch.Frequency", "Foraging.Mode", "Distribution", "Prefered.Habitat.Type")

ecological_filt_vars <- c("Mean.F.SVL.adults..mm.", "Mode.of.reproduction", "Clutch.Frequency", "Foraging.Mode", "Distribution", "Prefered.Habitat.Type")

#all variables
all_vars <- c(environmental_vars, ecological_all_vars)

all_filt_vars <- c(environmental_vars, ecological_filt_vars)

#now we have to make no NA datasets for all of these mixes
#first mean.clutch.size NAs
lizard_mcs_clean <- lizard %>%
  drop_na(Mean.Clutch.Size)

# Environmental variables
env_clean <- lizard %>%
  select(Mean.Clutch.Size, all_of(environmental_vars)) %>%
  drop_na()

# All ecological
ecological_all_clean <- lizard %>%
  select(Mean.Clutch.Size, all_of(ecological_all_vars)) %>%
  drop_na()

# Filtered ecological
ecological_filt_clean <- lizard %>%
  select(Mean.Clutch.Size, all_of(ecological_filt_vars)) %>%
  drop_na()

# All combined
all_clean <- lizard %>%
  select(Mean.Clutch.Size, all_of(all_vars)) %>%
  drop_na()

# Filtered combined
all_filt_clean <- lizard %>%
  select(Mean.Clutch.Size, all_of(all_filt_vars)) %>%
  drop_na()

#now we'll split into our training and testing sets, being careful to make sure that the species are spread evenly between the two groups
set.seed(123)

lizard_noNA <- lizard %>%
  drop_na()

split_clutch <- initial_split(lizard_noNA, prop = 0.75, strata = "Mean.Clutch.Size") #this allows us 

###need to think about what to do about repeat species eeeee

#tune the forest
params_CV <- trainControl(method = "cv", verboseIter = FALSE, number = 10)
```


```{r rf Model1 - environmental}

#to split our dataset into training and testing datasets
train_clutch <- analysis(split_clutch)
test_clutch <- assessment(split_clutch)


#random forest environmental all variables
randomForest(
  reformulate(environmental_vars, response = "Mean.Clutch.Size"),
  data = train_clutch,
  ntree = 500, 
  importance = TRUE) -> rf_env

#predictions
rf_env_predictions <- predict(rf_env, newdata = select(test_clutch, -Mean.Clutch.Size))
#check model performance (as regression)
caret::postResample(
  pred = rf_env_predictions,
  obs = test_clutch$Mean.Clutch.Size)
#check variable importance
varImpPlot(rf_env)

#tuning mtry
caret::train(
  reformulate(environmental_vars, response = "Mean.Clutch.Size"),
  data = na.omit(train_clutch[, c("Mean.Clutch.Size", environmental_vars)]),
  method = "rf",
  metric = "RMSE", #for regression, not classification
  trControl = params_CV,
  tuneGrid = expand.grid(mtry = 1:6),
  ntree = 500) -> clutch_environment

clutch_environment #mtry = 1? weird. why?? 
plot(clutch_environment)

M1_predictions <- predict(clutch_environment, newdata = test_clutch)

caret::postResample(
  pred = M1_predictions,
  obs = test_clutch$Mean.Clutch.Size) -> metrics_env

```


```{r rf Model2 - ecological all}
#first, we have to remove the NAs. 
train_eco <- train_clutch %>%
  select(Mean.Clutch.Size, all_of(ecological_all_vars)) %>%
  drop_na()

test_eco <- test_clutch %>%
  select(Mean.Clutch.Size, all_of(ecological_all_vars)) %>%
  drop_na()

#random forest eco
randomForest(
  reformulate(ecological_all_vars, response = "Mean.Clutch.Size"),
  data = train_eco,
  ntree = 500,
  importance = TRUE) ->  rf_eco_all

rf_eco_all_predictions <- predict(rf_eco_all, newdata = test_eco)

#check model performance (as regression)
caret::postResample(
  pred = rf_eco_all_predictions,
  obs = test_eco$Mean.Clutch.Size)

varImpPlot(rf_eco_all)

#train mtry
caret::train(
  reformulate(ecological_all_vars, response = "Mean.Clutch.Size"),
  data = na.omit(train_eco[, c("Mean.Clutch.Size", ecological_all_vars)]),
  method = "rf",
  metric = "RMSE",
  trControl = params_CV,
  tuneGrid = expand.grid(mtry = 1:length(ecological_filt_vars)),
  ntree = 500) -> clutch_ecological

clutch_ecological #mtry = 5
plot(clutch_ecological)

M2_predictions <- predict(clutch_ecological, newdata = test_eco)

caret::postResample(
  pred = M2_predictions,
  obs = test_eco$Mean.Clutch.Size) -> metrics_eco_all

```

```{r rf Model 3 - filtered ecological variables}
# First, remove NAs from the variables used in this model

train_eco_filt <- train_clutch %>%
  select(Mean.Clutch.Size, all_of(ecological_filt_vars)) %>%
  drop_na()

test_eco_filt <- test_clutch %>%
  select(Mean.Clutch.Size, all_of(ecological_filt_vars)) %>%
  drop_na()


# Random Forest: filtered ecological variables
randomForest(
  reformulate(ecological_filt_vars, response = "Mean.Clutch.Size"),
  data = train_eco_filt,
  ntree = 500,
  importance = TRUE) -> rf_eco_filt

# Predictions
rf_eco_filt_predictions <- predict(rf_eco_filt, newdata = test_eco_filt)

# Check model performance (regression)
caret::postResample(
  pred = rf_eco_filt_predictions,
  obs = test_eco_filt$Mean.Clutch.Size)

# Variable importance
varImpPlot(rf_eco_filt)

# Tune mtry
caret::train(
  reformulate(ecological_filt_vars, response = "Mean.Clutch.Size"),
  data = train_eco_filt,
  method = "rf",
  metric = "RMSE",
  trControl = params_CV,
  tuneGrid = expand.grid(
    mtry = 1:length(ecological_filt_vars)),
  ntree = 500) -> clutch_ecological_filt

# View optimized model
clutch_ecological_filt #mtry = 4

# Plot tuning results
plot(clutch_ecological_filt)

# Predictions from tuned model
M3_predictions <- predict(
  clutch_ecological_filt,
  newdata = test_eco_filt)

# Evaluate tuned model
caret::postResample(
  pred = M3_predictions,
  obs = test_eco_filt$Mean.Clutch.Size) -> metrics_eco_filt

```

```{r rf Model4 - all variables (not filtered)}
# First, remove NAs from the variables used in this model
train_all <- train_clutch %>%
  select(Mean.Clutch.Size, all_of(all_vars)) %>%
  drop_na()

test_all <- test_clutch %>%
  select(Mean.Clutch.Size, all_of(all_vars)) %>%
  drop_na()

# Random Forest: all variables
randomForest(
  reformulate(all_vars, response = "Mean.Clutch.Size"),
  data = train_all,
  ntree = 500,
  importance = TRUE) -> rf_all

# Predictions
rf_all_predictions <- predict(rf_all, newdata = test_all)

# Check model performance (regression)
caret::postResample(
  pred = rf_all_predictions,
  obs = test_all$Mean.Clutch.Size)

# Variable importance
varImpPlot(rf_all)

# Tune mtry
caret::train(
  reformulate(all_vars, response = "Mean.Clutch.Size"),
  data = train_all,
  method = "rf",
  metric = "RMSE",
  trControl = params_CV,
  tuneGrid = expand.grid(
    mtry = 1:length(all_vars)),
  ntree = 500) -> clutch_all

# View optimized model
clutch_all #mtry 11!

# Plot tuning results
plot(clutch_all)

# Predictions from tuned model
M4_predictions <- predict(clutch_all, newdata = test_all)

# Evaluate tuned model
caret::postResample(
  pred = M4_predictions,
  obs = test_all$Mean.Clutch.Size) -> metrics_all
```

```{r comparing random forests}
#ok, time to compare!
model_comparison <- rbind(
  Environmental = metrics_env,
  Ecological_all = metrics_eco_all,
  Ecological_filtered = metrics_eco_filt,
  Combined_all = metrics_all,
  Combined_filtered = metrics_all_filt)

model_comparison

# Lowest RMSE first
model_comparison[order(model_comparison[, "RMSE"]), ]

# Highest R-squared first
model_comparison[order(-model_comparison[, "Rsquared"]), ]

```
